item.title: POINT OF ORIGIN I Castaway Island Resort
item.description: ON July 6, 2026, Castaway Island Resort celebrated its 60th anniversary marking a significant milestone for the Mamanuca based retreat. Located on Qalito Island and facing the vast oceanic expanse of crystal blue waters, Castaway Island Resort has grown and established itself as one of Fiji’s beloved family resorts.
item.content:encoded:
ON July 6, 2026, Castaway Island Resort celebrated its 60th anniversary marking a significant milestone for the Mamanuca based retreat.

Located on Qalito Island and facing the vast oceanic expanse of crystal blue waters, Castaway Island Resort has grown and established itself as one of Fiji’s beloved family resorts.

Today, the resort covers about 17 acres of the private island and features a wide variety of facilities that has kept countless guests entertained over the past six decades.

So, for the uninitiated, it would come as a surprise that Castaway Island Resort’s origins started on July 6, 1966, with a single thatched bure.

The resort gained notoriety and momentum when it was bought by the late Geoff Shaw who later became an influential figure in Fiji’s tourism industry.

His footprints and influence spanned between the shores of the Mamanucas, Nadi and the Coral Coast.

In one of his last interviews with this masthead, Mr Shaw recalled his association with Castaway which began in the early 1990s when the resort was 26 years old.

“It was in 1992 and of course Castaway was in receivership that time so I thought there was an opportunity to see if I could purchase a property that was iconic in the Mamanuca region,” he said.

“My accountant thought I was crazy and he said how are you going to do this, you don’t have any money, but I had another little property in those days called the Reef Hotel.

“I had this idea back in those days that I wanted to, in fact, recreate what the Reef was and build it into what is today the Outrigger.”

Mr Shaw bought Castaway when it went into receivership and had a dream to convert the property into a family focused island getaway.

He had said the success of each project he undertook relied heavily on its people.

“It’s not just our product – our people make the product and with their support and dedication, taking ownership of what my vision was at that time.

Under the late Mr Shaw’s stewardship, Castaway Island became synonymous with authentic, barefoot island hospitality, a blueprint that drew guests back year after year and established the resort as one of the defining properties in Pacific tourism.

That legacy endures in the resort’s hosts, some of whom have worked on the island for more than 30 years, and in the guests who have made Castaway Island Resort a family tradition across generations.

In 2014, Castaway Island changed ownership after Mr Shaw sold the property to Outrigger Enterprises Group.

Castaway Enterprise Group was then acquired by Denver-based KSL Capital Partners LLC.

Under the present owners, the resort has grown into one of the Mamanuca island group’s most popular retreats amassing accolades at the Fiji Tourism Excellence Awards over the past two decades and a front runner in conservation efforts through the Mamanuca Environment Society and the Outrigger Resorts and Hotels led initiative Outrigger Zone.

According to the resort, the program allows the resort to focus on integrating the island’s ecosystem with the guest experience.

In 2025 alone, the resort launched a Sculptural Coral Gene Bank in partnership with non-profit Counting Coral which is a marine-grade steel installation housing more than 500 carefully selected parent corals and is designed to support the long-term regeneration of the surrounding reef.

The resort also collaborated in the translocation of 15 endangered Fijian Crested Iguanas to Qalito Island marking their return after more than 40 years.

Last year, Castaway became the second property in Fiji to earn the Green Key Certification signifying its commitment to sustainability and serving as an assurance for guests that it adheres to strict environmental requirements.

Resort general manager Steven Andrews said the resort offered a rare hospitality experience that’s more than a destination.

“It has allowed travellers to connect with each other and for generations of families to bond across six decades,” Mr Andrew said.

“The loyalty of our guests and the dedication of our hosts are a testament to what happens when a destination is built on authenticity.

“It’s the reason why our returnees and multigenerational families continue to call Castaway Island ‘home’.

“We’re proud to steward this legacy and are excited for everything the next decade holds as we invite more travellers to discover our island home for the first time.”

Later this year, the resort will kick start a week-long celebration themed around 1960s vintage and a nod to the era in which it was born.

A resort statement explained the program will include a traditional Fijian welcome ceremony, a Returnee Guest Appreciation Day, a Management Cocktail Evening, an Environment Day centred on coral planting and the Coral Gene Bank, and a Cocktail Gala on November 27.

Until then the resort introduced a guest and host driven storytelling campaign, inviting generations of loyal guests to share their favourite memories through photos, videos and personal reflections. The campaign will also spotlight longtime hosts whose stories have helped shape the resort’s enduring Bula spirit of hospitality.

item.title: BACK IN HISTORY I Significant milestone – Rewa Dairy opens UHT milk processing, packaging plant
item.description: Fiji’s dairy industry once stood at the heart of the nation’s drive toward self-sufficiency. One of its defining moments came with the official opening of the Rewa Co-operative Dairy Company’s Ultra Heat Treatment (UHT) milk processing and packaging plant, which marked a major step forward for local milk production.
item.content:encoded:
Fiji’s dairy industry once stood at the heart of the nation’s drive toward self-sufficiency.

One of its defining moments came with the official opening of the Rewa Co-operative Dairy Company’s Ultra Heat Treatment (UHT) milk processing and packaging plant, which marked a major step forward for local milk production.

According to a The Fiji Times article published on March 9, 1988, the inauguration was officiated by the then Minister for Primary Industries, Villame Gonelevu, who described the dairy industry as an essential pillar of Fiji’s economy and nutrition.

“The dairy industry is important to Fiji for its well-known product, milk, which is often called a complete food and consumed by all in one form or another,” Mr Gonelevu said.

At the time, Fiji was focused on reducing its dependence on imported dairy products while creating greater opportunities for local farmers.

The industry supplied milk and cream through about 200 registered dairy farms, with more than 75 per cent supplying Rewa Dairy.

The company collected almost 20,000 litres of milk and 10,000 kilograms of cream each day, producing a range of products including pasteurised milk, flavoured milk, butter, cheese, cultured dairy products and powdered milk.

The new Ultra Heat Treatment (UHT) plant enabled Rewa Dairy to package milk in long-life cartons that could be stored for up to six months without refrigeration before opening, making fresh-quality milk more accessible to rural communities and the outer islands.

Speaking at the opening ceremony, Mr Gonelevu emphasised the industry’s key objectives, which included increasing local milk production to improve national self-sufficiency, strengthening rural incomes, creating employment on dairy farms and in processing facilities, and improving the nutritional wellbeing of Fiji’s population.

The minister also praised Rewa Dairy for exceeding its projected milk production target despite the severe drought, describing the achievement as evidence of the industry’s resilience and promising future.

The launch of the UHT facility also had an immediate social impact.

During the ceremony, the minister unveiled a 900-litre gift pack of Rewa Life milk, which was distributed to families in need, symbolising the company’s commitment to supporting local communities.

For a long time, Rewa Dairy remained one of Fiji’s best-known food manufacturers, and the opening of its UHT processing plant stood as one of the company’s most significant milestones in the development of Fiji’s dairy industry.

The investment demonstrated how innovation, government support and the commitment of local farmers could work together to strengthen food security and reduce Fiji’s reliance on imported dairy products.

More than the opening of a new processing facility, the inauguration of the Ultra Heat Treatment (UHT) milk processing and packaging plant marked an important chapter in Fiji’s agricultural history and laid the foundation for a stronger and more resilient local dairy industry.

item.title: LOOK BACK I Thousands at funeral of family killed in crash
item.description: More than 4500 people crowded Wailoaloa Crematorium in Nadi to pay their last respects to a Nadi family of five killed in a road crash. The article was published in this newspaper on Thursday August 9, 1984.
item.content:encoded:
More than 4500 people crowded Wailoaloa Crematorium in Nadi to pay their last respects to a Nadi family of five killed in a road crash.

The article was published in this newspaper on Thursday August 9, 1984.

Several thousand earlier went to the family’s home at Nawaka where the bodies were placed in five separate coffins.

Relatives and friends wept openly as the coffins were put on a carrier which took them to the cemetery.

Killed in the crash at Semo, Sigatoka were Manik Raj, his wife Nirmal Wati, their son Manoj Kumar and daughters Vimal Kumari and Saroj Kumari.

They were driving back from Sigatoka after visiting relatives when their car collided with a Fiji Gas van coming from the opposite side.

Mr Raj was a maintenance foreman at Westgate Hotel while Manoj attended Shri Vivekananda High School, and his sisters attended Andrews Primary School in Nadi.

Teachers and students from the schools and hotel staff were among mourners at the funeral.

At the Wailoaloa crematorium, the bodies were taken out of the coffins and placed on a single pyre on the seashore.

Before the bodies were cremated people filed past to pay their last respects to the family.

Mr Raj left behind his mother and two sisters while Wati is survived by two brothers and four sisters.

Raj and Wati had been married for twenty years.

item.title: TRAVEL I Korovou’s best kept secret is back on the menu
item.description: THERE is no need for mad rush in the laid-back township of Korovou. Here the clock seems to tik tok a little slower, reminding keen travellers that some of Fiji’s unforgettable experiences are found tucked away from the city’s hurried pace.
item.content:encoded:
THERE is no need for mad rush in the laid-back township of Korovou.

Here the clock seems to tik tok a little slower, reminding keen travellers that some of Fiji’s unforgettable experiences are found tucked away from the city’s hurried pace.

Drive into the heart of Tailevu North and, perched above the township with sweeping views of the lush countryside, sits the newly renovated Tailevu Hotel, a familiar landmark that is rewriting a new chapter.

For years, the hotel has been a resting place for weary travellers, government workers and families passing through the district.

Today, it is giving people another reason to stop, not just for the night, but for a memorable meal.

Step inside and the first thing you notice is the warmth.

There is no pretence in the air – just genuine Fijian hospitality from a small team that welcomes guests with easy smiles and attentive service.

Then comes the food. The new breakfast, lunch and dinner menu is a celebration of Tailevu itself, fresh, generous and proudly local. Every plate reflects the abundance of the province, where organic vegetables grow in nearby farms, fish arrive fresh from the coast and traditional recipes continue to be passed from one generation to the next.

Behind the menu is chef Asupa Leba, who believes good food should be accessible to everyone.

Before taking charge of the kitchen in Korovou, the Totoya, Lau islander honed her skills at the Shangri-La Fijian Resort on the Coral Coast before moving on to some of Suva’s well-known cafés and coffee houses.

Those experiences shaped her appreciation for quality dining, but it was Korovou that perhaps inspired her latest creation.

“I walked around town to see what people were eating,” she said.

“I realised there wasn’t a place where families could enjoy affordable fine dining in a beautiful setting. That’s what inspired this menu.”

It is a philosophy that is reflected in every dish. Breakfast begins with a generous big breakfast – crispy toast, fluffy omelette, sausages and perfectly cooked bacon, of course with your favoursite choice of juice or hot beverage.

It is simple, hearty and satisfying, with plans already underway to introduce more traditional Fijian breakfast favourites.

By lunchtime, the kitchen is in full swing. One dish, in particular, tells the story of Tailevu better than words ever could.

For just $18, the catch-of-the-day platter brings together crispy fried fish, stuffed freshwater mussels, creamy kokoda, fresh miti ota, comforting rourou balls with a tuna filling and golden eggplant fritters.

Every bite is a reminder that Fiji’s finest ingredients often come from its own backyard.

As the afternoon sun softens over Korovou and the hills begin to glow, dinner offers another taste of home.

A steaming bowl of tender sui served alongside fresh rourou or moca is comfort food at its best—rich, wholesome and deeply rooted in local tradition. Alternatively, you might like to sink into fish cooked in rich coconut cream.

But the experience doesn’t end at the dining table.

Enjoy a refreshing drink at the nearby bar before heading into the hotel’s dance hall, where locals and visitors alike gather as familiar island tunes fill the air.

It’s the kind of place where strangers quickly become friends, and where an evening can effortlessly stretch into a night of laughter, music and dancing.

In many ways, the Tailevu Hotel mirrors the township around it. It is unassuming with its attractions and full of surprises too. For travellers making their way along Kings Road, the hotel is more than a convenient stopover.

It is a chance to slow down, enjoy honest food prepared by Ms Leba and her team, and experience the warmth of a community that has always known how to make visitors feel at home.

Sometimes the best journeys are not about racing to the next destination but a warm welcome, a beautifully prepared meal and a place that reminds you why you chose to travel in the first place.

That place is Korovou, where the Tailevu Hotel is ready to embrace you, breakfast, lunch and dinner!!

The hotel billboard can be clearly seen the from Kings Road. Picture: ANA MADIGIBULI

The catch-of-the-day platter. Picture: ANA MADIGIBULI

A diner at lunch. Picture: ANA MADIGIBULI

item.title: COMMUNITY WORK I Blessings on the trail back to Lavena
item.description: A PROMISE made in the aftermath of one of Fiji’s darkest moments is about to come full circle. Ten years after witnessing the destruction left behind by Tropical Cyclone Winston in Lavena, Taveuni, Warrane College Dean Alex Perrottet is returning, this time not as a journalist documenting tragedy, but leading a group of university students determined to lend a helping hand.
item.content:encoded:
A PROMISE made in the aftermath of one of Fiji’s darkest moments is about to come full circle.

Ten years after witnessing the destruction left behind by Tropical Cyclone Winston in Lavena, Taveuni, Warrane College Dean Alex Perrottet is returning, this time not as a journalist documenting tragedy, but leading a group of university students determined to lend a helping hand.

For the students at Warrane College, the upcoming work camp is more than a volunteer project. It is an opportunity to step beyond the classroom, immerse themselves in village life and contribute to improvements that they hope will leave a lasting impact on Lavena Primary School.

For Mr Perrottet however, the journey begins with a promise.

“When I visited Lavena as a journalist straight after Cyclone Winston in 2016, the whole village was ruined,” he recalls.

“At that time, I promised the turaga ni koro I would return one day with a volunteer group. So, 10 years later here we are.”

Mr Perrottet has organised numerous volunteer projects in Fiji over the years including in Ra and the Yasawa Islands, but this will be the college’s first project in Lavena.

He believes community service benefits everyone involved.

“These projects are a win-win,” he said.

“It gives us a great purpose in the college, and it helps everyone to give generously and then we have an amazing cultural immersion in Fiji and can actually make a difference to the school.”

The work planned for Lavena Primary School focuses on practical improvements that will benefit students long after the volunteers have returned home.

“These are projects that the community just wouldn’t get to normally,” he said.

“It means the school students can eat together under a shelter during the school day and also be kept safe and secure within the school grounds.”

Mr Perrottet acknowledged those who helped make the project possible.

“We’re very grateful to head teacher, Luke Naisuludriu for working with us on this project and being so keen to make it happen.

“We also have a number of Warrane and UNSW alumni in Fiji and we’re very grateful to the assistance of Kirit Patel from Motibhai Group, Michael Yee Joy and Ioane Naiveli in Suva and Josefa Wivou in Nadi.

“These are esteemed old boys who are still in contact with Warrane and proud to see Warrane come to Fiji.”

For social director Will Hadley, the trip carries a different meaning.

The actuarial studies student from Newcastle has visited Fiji five times before, but always as a tourist.

“I have great memories of dancing and drinking with strangers and how easily they made me feel like family,” he said.

“However, I’ve always come as a tourist. This is the first time I get to give something back.”

He said Fiji had left a lasting impression on him through friendships and experiences accumulated over several visits.

“Fiji has meant so much to me over the years. I’ve made great friendships and had some amazing memories.

“The chance to go back and actually contribute to something like this means so much to me. Taveuni is new to me, and I think seeing village life properly will change how I see the country.”

Second-year engineering student Christian de Jersey is equally eager for the experience.

As Warrane’s sports director and a key member of the college’s Oz-tag team, he hopes to spend time with Lavena students and learn Fiji’s style of one-touch rugby.

“I’m also very excited about the opportunity to contribute to the Lavena community and work alongside everyone involved,” he said.

“Hopefully, we can make a positive difference and do a great job.”

The college is also donating new rugby uniforms for the school’s teams, something Christian is particularly looking forward to presenting.

“This experience is going to mean a great deal to us, and we hope it will be meaningful for everyone in Lavena.

item.title: DISCOVERING FIJI I After the silence – Death was not the end
item.description: THE death of Reverend Thomas Baker in the highlands of Viti Levu has become one of Fiji’s most enduring historical stories, its significance reaching far beyond the events of his final day. More than 150 years later, it is the legacy that followed which continues to resonate.
item.content:encoded:
THE death of Reverend Thomas Baker in the highlands of Viti Levu has become one of Fiji’s most enduring historical stories, its significance reaching far beyond the events of his final day.

More than 150 years later, it is the legacy that followed which continues to resonate.

His life ended in 1867, but the years that came after gave rise to remembrance and acts of reconciliation that would span generations.

Pieces of his story surfaced in churches, museums, old newspaper archives and even beneath the floorboards of the Baker Memorial Hall in Davuilevu.

A pair of worn boots, a tabua offered in atonement, a single bone carefully preserved and buried, and letters written in his own hand became enduring reminders of a missionary whose death marked one of the most significant moments in Fiji’s Christian history.

Rather than fading into history, Baker’s memory continued to shape the Methodist Church in Fiji and became part of the nation’s historical record.

His legacy was carried not only by those who knew him, but also by those who inherited the responsibility of remembering.

Long after Baker’s death, those who had worked alongside him remembered him not simply the way he died, but for the character with which he lived.

In a paper presented before the Fijian Society on July 10, 1909, Reverend A.J. Small described Baker as a man whose greatest qualities lay in both his intellect and his heart.

“Thomas Baker was the fortunate possessor of many fine qualities of mind and heart,” Rev. Small said.

He described him as “sagacious, tactful, broad-minded, courageous, enthusiastic and devoted.”

Although he noted Baker was “not a scholar in the strict sense of the word”, Rev. Small believed he possessed a deep understanding of the people among whom he worked.

“As a Fijian speaker he took high rank, while his knowledge of native habits and customs was said to have been unique,” he said.

According to Rev. Small that understanding often proved invaluable during the difficult years of missionary work.

“Again, and again this special knowledge coupled with his unfailing tactfulness, saved him and his followers in those far away dark days.”

What stood out most however, was Baker’s unwavering commitment to his calling.

“Mr Baker was also a man of inflexible purpose. The path of duty once made clear to him no power on earth could turn him from it.”

For Rev. Small, Baker’s life could be summed up in a single image.

“Having lit his torch at the altar of the skies he marched boldly forward to do and die like the brave knight he was.”

His words became one of the earliest tributes to Baker’s legacy, shifting attention away from the tragedy of his death and towards the life he had dedicated to missionary work.

While Baker never returned home, the letters he left behind survived him.

Written only days before his death, they revealed not a man anticipating martyrdom, but one determined to complete the work he believed he had been called to do.

In a letter to his colleague, Reverend Jesse Carey, Baker wrote of his intention to continue across the island.

“I do not fear the natives, and we hope to do them good.”

The letter reflected both confidence and conviction.

Rather than expressing fear, Baker focused on the journey ahead and the communities he hoped to reach.

His final letter to his wife carried a more personal tone.

“I wish to do the people good,” he wrote.

He asked her to “cheer up and pray for me”, assuring her that he was “on my Master’s work.”

He spoke affectionately of their children, asking her to “kiss the children for me, all of them and tell them to pray for me.”

item.title: REFLECTION I Seeking refuge in the mask
item.description: This poem was composed from a challenging perspective, as it was written about a friend who shared the trials and tribulations of a sad life journey with me. Alas, she resides abroad and I felt that my offer of comfort and compassion towards her situation was subdued in depth due to our distance. item.content:encoded:
This poem was composed from a challenging perspective, as it was written about a friend who shared the trials and tribulations of a sad life journey with me. Alas, she resides abroad and I felt that my offer of comfort and compassion towards her situation was subdued in depth due to our distance.

Thus, the inspiration for this poem as an Ode to her true character – her dedication to duty, her resolve to stay through the years rather than walk away and even today, live life with a face of Grace, despite enduring many chapters of conflict.

People seek recourse to a mask for many reasons.

Some attempt to conceal negative energy – a narcissistic personality.

Some seek refuge in a mask as a medium for healing a hurt heart, without attention or detection.

Others may seek recourse to a mask to preserve and protect their positive energy – a face of serene silence in the midst of turbulent tides that wash their way.

The poem sought to assure a long-suffering heart that there are people with eyes that see. There are people with ears that listen. There are people with minds that reflect from observation the reality of a situation.

It is a life of torment for those who live a life confined within a frame and a test for those who walk beside their path in faithful friendship. The conviction of their conditioning – often self-inflicted from doubt and depression – is referred to as ‘Belief Perseverance’ in social psychology and sadly, a perplexing phenomenon which provides an explanation on why some people are protective of their initial beliefs.

They preserve their beliefs even when offered new, truthful and sometimes contradictory avenues and evidence to change the course of their life path. Indeed, it is a challenge to convince them to heal from within of their own accord and in their own time. Nonetheless, an understanding of the belief bias system is an aid to understanding their social sensitivity and delicate decision-making process.

The principal perspectives of belief perseverance focus on two key factors:

1. Cognitive dissonance – people feel distress due to holding two or more opposing beliefs.

2. Confirmation bias – to eliminate feelings of distress, people may neglect new beliefs that are not aligned to their current beliefs. Thus, they dismiss advice and evidence that can restrain and resolve a negative situation.

My friend neither sought professional assistance and intervention or shared her experiences with anyone, until our correspondence matured with time. Her solution was to seek refuge in Nature and continue to be the soldier on duty, as per her belief system from childhood socialisation.

I composed the poem as a personal initiative to instigate healing from within and hopefully, she would realise her worth one day to initiate positive change. Unfortunately, as time passed, I noted that the belief perseverance syndrome was so well imbedded in her personality that it was akin more to an infestation – waves of negative emotions would invade her mind on a regular basis to the extent that she withdrew into episodes of deep depression.

Before I composed the poem, I appended a card to my regular correspondence. It was a plain card with a message I only came to realise later, would create a profound impact. The message read: “You Are Enough.” That was the only sentence on the card. The response to me was: “Thank You.”

I was both surprised and pleased by the response I received because it relayed to me many words unspoken. She likely received that message for the first time in her life and after reflecting on her response, I composed the poem.

Suffice to say, she has chosen the path of self-healing.

item.title: FOCUS I A farewell in song – As Pacific treasures prepare for a new chapter
item.description: Prayer, song and dance echoed through the South Australian Museum’s Pacific Cultures Gallery as Pacific communities gathered not to say goodbye forever, but to honour the beginning of a new journey. The occasion, known as the Melanesian Lullaby, marked an emotional milestone for one of Australia’s most significant collections of Pacific cultural heritage.
item.content:encoded:
Prayer, song and dance echoed through the South Australian Museum’s Pacific Cultures Gallery as Pacific communities gathered not to say goodbye forever, but to honour the beginning of a new journey.

The occasion, known as the Melanesian Lullaby, marked an emotional milestone for one of Australia’s most significant collections of Pacific cultural heritage.

Hosted by the Papua New Guinea Association of South Australia in partnership with the South Australian Museum, the gathering symbolised a gentle farewell as thousands of treasured cultural objects entered a planned period of rest and conservation.

Like the lullaby that inspired the event, the ceremony represented comfort, protection and care, a promise that the stories carried by the objects would continue long after they leave public view.

From Monday, August 3, 2026, the Pacific Cultures Gallery temporarily closed after decades on display, beginning a major conservation and cultural care program that the Museum says will protect the collection for generations to come.

The gallery had remained open until Sunday, August 2, allowing visitors one final opportunity to experience the exhibition before work commenced.

The South Australian Museum houses Australia’s largest collection of Pacific material, with around 3,000 bows, arrows, spears, shields, utensils, ornaments, masks and ritual objects from Papua New Guinea, the Solomon and Santa Cruz Islands, Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji and New Zealand.

Rather than marking an end, museum leaders say the closure signals the start of a new chapter.

South Australian Museum director Dr Samantha Hamilton said the decision reflected the Museum’s responsibility to care for objects that hold deep spiritual and cultural significance.

“I’ve had the privilege of being taught by elders and by youths on the importance of cultural materials,” she said.

“My role here at the museum is to bring all cultures together and to create a space where the South Australian community, but also the people of Australia, can share stories, knowledge and respect for each other’s culture.

For Dr Hamilton, the collection represents far more than museum pieces.

“These objects absolutely represent spiritual and cultural values, the power of the people who created them and so it’s our responsibility to now be able to put these objects to rest,” she said.

“They have been on display for decades. The wonderful Centennial Hut has been on display since 1936 and it’s time to be responsible and actually put it to rest so that future generations can also protect, preserve and learn from it.”

The conservation program will be undertaken in partnership with local Pacific communities, ensuring cultural authority, traditional knowledge and ceremonial protocols guide the care and stewardship of ancestral objects.

While the gallery doors have temporarily closed, Dr Hamilton stressed that public access to knowledge will continue through extensive documentation and digital technology.

“We are going to be creating digital records for people, for things that are in storage,” she said.

The Museum plans to create high-resolution 3D digitisations of objects, allowing people to continue engaging with the collection while conservation work progresses.

The reopening, planned for the coming years after the conservation program is completed will feature stronger community voices, broader representation of Pacific cultures and more contemporary storytelling.

For Adelaide resident and community leader of the Fijian Association of South Australia, Luke Qovu Junior, the Museum’s approach recognises what these objects truly represent.

“It is a great initiative by the South Australian Museum to preserve these cultural items for the future,” he said.

“Whilst embarking on this project they have collectively involved Pasifika communities that have strong connections and values to these artefacts, which hold profound cultural and ancestral significance to them, especially us Fijians.”

Mr Qovu said the collection carried meaning that extends far beyond history.

“For many Fijians, these artefacts represent more than history. They connect families to their provinces, villages, mataqali and yavusa. They remind us of the values passed down through generations, respect, service, courage, unity and faith.”

He said each object served as a tangible connection between past and present.

“They are physical reminders of who we are and where we come from. They are living connections to our ancestors.

“They tell the story of our people, our vanua, our customs and traditions, our way of life, our spirituality, our craftsmanship, our chiefs, our provinces, our kingdoms and the many generations that shaped the Fiji we know today.”

He said the Fijian community looked forward to working alongside the museum during the next stage of the project.

Hosted by the Papua New Guinea Association of South Australia in partnership with the South Australian Museum, the gathering symbolised a gentle farewell as thousands of treasured cultural objects entered a planned period of rest and conservation. Picture: SOUTH AUSTRALIAN MUSEUM / SIA DUFF

The conservation program will be undertaken in partnership with local Pacific communities, ensuring cultural authority, traditional knowledge and ceremonial protocols. Picture: SOUTH AUSTRALIAN MUSEUM
